utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, registrar, call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is the 9th of May, 2007. My greetings to all people present in the courtroom. Good morning, Mr. Scott. You're back with us. Good morning, Witness. Good morning, Defence counsel, and all the accused as well as all the people in the courtroom. Mr. Registrar you have some IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. OTP responds to the list of documents tendered by the Defence teams through witness Lizde Alija shall be given Exhibit number IC 542. 5D has also submitted a response to the OTP objections regarding the exhibits tendered through the witness Lizde Alija, and that shall be given Exhibit number 543. Finally, Prosecution has resubmitted a list of documents to be tendered through witness Herbert Okun, and that list shall be given Exhibit number 544. And also 1D has submitted a list of documents to be tendered through witness Herbert Okun and shall be assigned Exhibit number 545. That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Cross-examination is going to continue. I'm now giving the floor to Mr. Praljak, who is going to proceed with his cross-examination which he started yesterday. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness answers.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, good morning. I'd like to continue, and I'd like to have 00347 up on the screen, please. It's a map and on that map I'm going to ask you to look at some things. 3D 00347 is the number. Witness, yesterday you drew the position of the house in which you were located in East Mostar yesterday on that big map, although the map is not very legible, but on the one we have here today -- no, that doesn't seem to be the number. I want 3D 00347, and then 3D 14005. 3D 14/005 is the next number. Perhaps this would be faster if I were to put it up on the ELMO, because otherwise I'm afraid we're going to lose quite a lot of time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, on the ELMO. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we ought to wait for the map in colour. It's much more visible, because unfortunately on this one you can't see my markings. So can we have the map I asked for shown on e-court, please. I've given the numbers twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... back to the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the only map I have under that reference 3D 00347 is the one that appeared already on e-court, which is the view from -- of the lake. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's go back to the ELMO then, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you can see it better on this map, I think. You can see the Neretva River. Can we pan out a bit so that we can see the whole area, or zoom in, rather. No, pan out. Yes, yes. That will be fine. A little more, please. Do you agree that the separation line along the Bulevar up to Spanski Square and then Santic Street is the area marked, and was that, to your knowledge, indeed the separation line? Up at the top it says HVO on the left and the BH army on the right.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- sorry, yes, I do agree that was the separation line as I knew it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And at the top there you can see the main road that you mentioned running from Sarajevo to Metkovici, and it's in blue. Would you now mark on the map -- you said that the house that you lived in was above the road going eastwards. Could you now, looking at the Tito Bridge, which is the first bridge you can see here, indicate where your house was exactly, how far of above the main Sarajevo-Metkovici road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you have located the place where the house was, then we'll put the map back on the ELMO unless you find it difficult to remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I actually do find it difficult to actually pinpoint the house. Obviously the terrain was a little bit confused at the time, but I would put a mark here at about the -- about the level of the house, as I remember. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Would you put a number 1 there, please.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you put a 2 by the Tito Bridge. So number 2 for the Tito Bridge down there, please. It's the first bridge as you go in a straight line from your house westward.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in continuation we come to Spanish Square. You said yesterday that the distance from the HVO lines, and Their Honours know this from earlier testimony, we had a sniper expert in court, so from the first HVO lines to your house it was 1.500 metres, the distance. Is that right? Would that be the distance?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I would agree that that would be the approximate distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You're a professional soldier, and as we've heard here, you are a trained sniper shooter, and sniper shooters can shoot at a range of about 800 metres as being the ultimate range for highly professional people to hit their target. Would 800 metres be an acceptable sort of range?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, firstly I must correct you. I am not a recognised sniper shooter at all. Far from it. If you recall, I was an engineering officer in the Royal New Zealand Navy during my time there. The range of small arms, the -- the extremes of small arm range as I see it, a very extreme would be around 2.000. However, the accuracy of that range would be debatable or poor, rather. Eight hundred, I imagine, would be a reasonably short range for a -- a good sniper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to refer to the statement you gave to the Prosecutor, and point 44 of that statement where you say that fire came at you from the building that was well known as the bank and was a stronghold, and -- and, "In my opinion it was only the HVO that opened fire at us and not the BH army. And sometimes sniper fire would be opened at us while we were going up the stairs to the front of the building in which we were located, so that it is thanks to our luck and the fact that we were outside the range." So in your opinion, you were beyond that range. Is that correct? Is it correct what you say in your statement, that you were outside that range? And it is only because of good luck and the long range that no one was hit, you say.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my general assessment of why we were so lucky. And the -- I guess the firing from the bank, and I haven't got my statement before me at this point in time, but the firing from the bank in particular was when we were travelling down the road from the Tito Bridge, and in fact that was very, very close in a -- when it happened to myself, and two days later a Spanish soldier was killed by the same sniper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In your statement, sir, in paragraph 63 of the 25th of September of the daily report you say that some shells fell in the hospital -- "some shells landed in the hospital area. I think that the ABiH setting up mortars in close proximity to the hospital inspired in action by the HVO. In general, the shelling from west to east was concentrated on the front lines." That's the first part. And then towards the end you go on to say the following: "Initially when we moved into the accommodations in East Mostar, the ABiH would set up weapons within 15 metres of our place, which of course attracted HVO fire." Can you confirm the fact, and maybe later on if we have time I'll go into this, that the BH army did have mortars placed in the vicinity of the hospital? Can you confirm that? That's the first part of my question.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm they did at times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you also confirm that according to what it says here, and later on you go on to say something to that effect as well, that in your vicinity where you were that they would is set up their own mortars or anti-tank -- 20-millimetre anti-tank guns?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest that was only very initially when we first moved in there probably within the first week, and we soon got that sorted out. I think my -- and I'm not too sure why I said 15 metres there. I think that's a little bit short. But nevertheless, they did set up some weapons in the first week that we were there, and to my knowledge they didn't reappear at any time, or I can't recall it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the next document, 3D 00913. But before we have a look at that, would you place your signature and date on the map that we've just looked at. Thank you. And the next document, please, is 3D 00913.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll first have an IC number for the map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this map will become Exhibit IC 546. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 3D 00913. And it is a response to a letter from the observers from Medjugorje. The date is the 3rd of November, 1993, signed by the commander -- or, rather, a representative. Well, it was signed by Raguz, and it was signed on behalf of Mr. Lasic, commander of the operative zone. Could you take a look at that. It's a response to the protest letter. Would you please read it, and I'd just like to focus on paragraph 2, and it says: "In reference to that, the HVO from its highest instance issued orders and instructions about the conduct of its units and their members towards the members of the international organisations." And then it says: "These orders and instructions have been issued to all units. In addition to that, these problems have been pointed out verbally many times during meetings of commanders, and the soldiers were also informed in the appropriate way through the newspaper Aktualnosti," et cetera, et cetera. But would you go further down the text, and it says: "The command asked the military observers not to let MOS soldiers gather around the house in which they stay, as was the case so far, as has been the case so far." Now, Witness, can you tell us whether there was any gathering of BH army soldiers in -- in groups around the house or in the vicinity of your house or in front your house for any reason whatsoever? Did they gather together?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never witnessed it. I don't -- I don't -- to my knowledge, and I'm saying from my own point of view and from what was reported to me, I have no knowledge of that happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak. In the English translation of this letter they speak of MOS soldiers. I thought that might be referred to as military observers. Are you saying that this is an abbreviation for ABiH soldiers? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, let me ask the witness the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that there were Mujahedin in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never witnessed any Mujahedin activity in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that apart from the BH army units in Mostar there was parallel activity and action from the Muslim armed forces, which to a large extent were under the control of religious leaders or religious officials, and their name was MOS, the Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only reference I have to -- to their activities was as mentioned yesterday, which was north of the -- or in the Konjic area. Certainly within Mostar itself there was no knowledge of that by myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I think your question was not really answered, because I interrupted for the explanation. And I will recall the question is whether it is true, Mr. Finlayson, that ABiH soldiers used to gather around the house where the MO had their headquarters, the famous house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's negative. They -- they didn't gather in groups. I must say that there was one soldier living in the downstairs part of the house, and obviously other houses were in close proximity, but around those and around the UNMO house there was no gathering of the BiH soldiers or any other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Given your answer, Witness, there is some degree of -- of ambiguity. There was a soldier who lived in the downstairs part of the house, but a soldier from whose -- which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: BiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand properly, there was an ABiH soldier who lived in the same house as you did. This ABiH soldier, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was dressed in normal combat gear most of the time, as were all the others in the -- in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you yourself, how were you dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In combat gear with the blue hat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we assume the following situation: Some 1.500 metres away from the house that there is an HVO soldier with binoculars, and he observes the house, and he sees an ABiH soldier in camouflage gear. How can he make the difference between a UN member, also in combat gear with a helmet or without a helmet, and how can he make the difference between the UN soldier and other one before he shoots? Do you have an answer for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a fair comment. I would just say that most of the shootings in this -- their vicinity, if not all of them, occurred immediately after the UN vehicle had pulled up into the driveway. So bringing their attention to the fact that there was activity there. The other thing was the fact that the shots through the window which I described yesterday was generally also upon the first passing through that window of UNMOs after their arrival, although that wasn't always the case. I'm assuming that they were also using scopes on their rifle, but I wouldn't be able to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question. This ABiH soldier, was he armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At times he -- he would have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand properly, the UNMOs have settled in a building in which there was a soldier belonging to one of warring factions since there was a conflict at the time. Is this the situation that you are describing to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. It's not ideal, and at the time of moving into the accommodation it was discussed in detail with the headquarters in West Mostar as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But wasn't the solution, say, to the soldier to that he should move out so that there should be no confusion between the UN and a soldier who belonged to a warring faction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you need to understand that the soldier didn't typically hang around the front of the building. They -- they moved in different manner to us. If they moved out, yes, that could have been an option. We don't believe that that was why we were being sniped directly at every time the UN arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a very brief question. Indeed, in the document, Mr. Lasic complained about people gathering or, rather, about MOS soldiers gathering. Can you confirm that this soldier, who lived in the same building as you did, did not receive any visit, because it did happen that the visit he would receive from his fellow soldiers could be read as a gathering of ordinary people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can honestly not recall any gathering of soldiers. There would -- I -- I would see neighbours passing or whatever, and obviously conversation and in passing way together. However, no gathering was ever observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there was never any visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were individuals, possibly in the evening time, but no gathering. And I would easily -- and I would also firmly say that the shots at the UNMOs never coincided with any activity of the -- the soldier or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any apologies. I just wanted to say that this term, the term "gathering," this particular document does not denote any sort of official gathering of the BH army or any of their units. It's about individuals coming to an area or to a building in order to socialise for their own private purposes. That's the only thing that I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed after the questions by the Judges, because it was necessary to clear this out. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, sir, can you please tell me this: Were you ever fired at by a tank shell, a mortar shell, by howitzers, by tanks, or anti-aircraft guns? Were you ever targeted with any of these weapons ever?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Suppose the HVO wanted you to leave. You lived in Medjugorje. You had your own HQ there, and that was an area controlled by the HVO. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the headquarters and -- sorry. At the time of SMO, being when I was senior military officer there, I had my headquarters in Medjugorje as the main headquarters for BH South was always in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say whether you had any difficulty in going about your work while in Medjugorje, any particular incidents, your vehicles being targeted, lots of provocation, any sort of nuisance or unpleasant situations at all?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Medjugorje, travelling around through Citluk we would often have items, rocks and whatever, thrown at our vehicles. Medjugorje itself we had isolated cases. However, we -- we discarded those as isolated cases. We didn't worry too much. But Citluk was a particularly difficult area to work through as was at times West Mostar, but it never got to the -- the extremes. I think I mentioned in my diary I -- I envisaged it to be something similar to what I thought Northern Ireland would have been where you didn't quite know where to turn your back. The main concern with working from Medjugorje was the restrictions we had had on access into Mostar at times, which was talked about yesterday. Around the May time, when there is activity, we were prohibited in going in to observe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, sir. We should specify the date, of course, that sort of thing. Unfortunately, I don't have time to go into that now. Can we please move into closed session? I will be dropping a set of questions, but then let me go through your diary. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May have closed session for that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: P 00755 contains specific instructions to military observers. It runs into quite a number of pages, and the page I'm interested in is page 10 in the Croatian version, item 8, where it says: "Relations with the local population. In order to preserve the impression of not siding with either party, the UNMOs should show that their attitude towards the local population is a professional one. They should do their best not to entertain any close links with any individuals or organisations." Sir, was this part of the instructions that you received in relation to how you were supposed to relate to either of the parties involved in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I've never seen that document. However, I believe that most of our relationships were with the people we were living with. As you are aware, the brandy and the rakija is part of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, sir. Thank you. You've never seen the document. That's quite sufficient for my purposes, so I wouldn't like to delve any further into that. Can you please take these two documents to the ELMO? I'm now going back to the incident on Aleksa Santica Street. These two documents if possible. On Aleksa Santica Street you were car was hit from the back by bullets, which in your statement you ascertain had been fired by the HVO. First of all, that sketch that you showed the Chamber or the OTP, can we have that placed on the ELMO, please. It's a sketch that you drew. Can we look at the whole thing, please, the sketch in its entirety? The whole sketch. With your permission, sir, I drew the Bulevar, and I moved the school building, the gymnasium, to the other side of the Bulevar. Would you agree with that amendment, sir? It was on this side of the Bulevar and not on the lower side, not further down. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I must emphasise I did not draw that sketch, but, yes, I do agree. From my memory, it was on the other side of the Bulevar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to that, I drew the confrontation line right here. This is where you were moving, and it says here that this was an HVO controlled territory. Would you agree with me that the HVO were positioned to the right of the line along which you moved? However, you moved in this direction, and the HVO was always to your left and the BH army to your right. So we have the HVO above that line that I marked, which is the line along which you moved, and the HVO weren't there. Do you agree that this was the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We have to be clear here that this was an incident where Mr. Finlayson was not in the car moving. It seems that Mr. Praljak is insinuating that it was Mr. Finlayson in the vehicle moving, which is not the case, and I just want to make that clear. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I never said that Mr. Finlayson was in the vehicle. All I said was that he testified here that this vehicle was hit at the number 2 in this sketch from the back, and he said quite explicitly that the bullet had been fired by the HVO. If we look at the number 2, and that is the upper part of the street, that was under the control of the HVO, whereas the lower part of the street, this entire area was under the BH army. Since we shifted the school building in this sketch, could you please sign the sketch now and sign the correction or the amendment, and then we can move on to the next image.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correction of the front line I am unclear on, to be honest. Yeah. So I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. All right. Let's move on to the next image, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just have a question. On the -- this sketch on the right side that is circle. Does -- that circle, what does it mean? What is the meaning of this circle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's been added to the drawing, Your Honour, but I -- it's just circling where I believe it was indicated where the shot came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And where would the vehicle be at the moment it was hit? Is that indicated on this sketch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's indicated by 3, 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That would be halfway down this road. Right. Thank you. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Finlayson, what about this circle that I drew? The upper part of Aleksa Santica Street marked in red was being held by the HVO, and the lower part of that street and the area in which this vehicle was moving was being held by the BH army. So within the circle itself the upper portion of the circle was being held by the BH army and the lower part by the HVO. Can you confirm that, sir, please, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't confirm that. In fact, just you bringing it up has maybe caused a bit of confusion in my own mind. I'll be thinking about it, though. But at this stage, my understanding was as it was drawn originally by the person who drew the sketch was that the HVO actually went across that street at that point. However, I would not sit here and say categorically that that was the case, now you've raised doubt, but certainly that was my opinion, my understanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Next one, please. Sir, we've had witnesses here who drew very accurate maps. Could you please turn it round. No, the other way. Vertically. HVO. Upside down. That's right. Please have a look, sir. This is the situation. We even agree with the Prosecutor on the front confrontation line. This is the red line marking the Bulevar that -- lower down from where it says HVO, and then there's the street that you pointed out to us. You head right from there and my drawing is quite accurate the BH army controlling this area and this other area under the control of the HVO. So is it true that you were moving along this Bulevar, to your left was always the HVO, you enter this small street and to your right is the BH army, and then you take another turn and drive into Aleksa Santica Street. At the very corner and we've had many witnesses testifying to that, on the one side of the street were the HVO units and facing them across the way were the BH army units. Please, a brief answer. Just say, "Yes, I do know that for a fact," or, "No, I don't know that," and then I'll move on and ask you another question.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us assume that the fire came from this corner, as Judge Trechsel asked. For what possible reasons? Somebody's in this vehicle and behind them at a distance of about 20 metres there is a face-off between the HVO and the BH army, both positioned behind this vehicle. With what degree of certainty did your men conclude that the shot had come from the HVO? Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber the logic behind that particular piece of reasoning? It's the circle that I drew in the last sketch, that's what I'm referring to. So you travel this whole way. The HVO are on your left and they're not firing. And then suddenly you arrive at this corner with the HVO and the BH army facing each other across the street. A bullet comes at you from behind, and you conclude that the bullet came from the HVO. Can you please disclose the logic behind this reasoning to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that the shooting started as soon as they rounded that corner, and at that time they were veering to the left to avoid the obstruction out -- protruding out from the -- the building, which in fact put their vehicle slightly at an angle towards the HVO. However, I was not on -- in the vehicle, so I can only take the report I -- I got as being accurate. But certainly that's -- and that would be logical looking at the sketch too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what you just told Judge Trechsel, the place where the fire started coming. This wasn't the corner itself. It was perhaps 10 or 15 metres from the corner itself. If you don't know, why don't you say, "I don't know there is no logic that I can possibly use to explain this." Why can't you just simply say? You are a soldier, sir, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With a pointer could you tell us where the vehicle was standing when it was hit by the bullet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I would prefer to refer to the report that came with that -- with that -- with that drawing. But -- because I've forgotten the wording of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have a sketch here, and this is probably a Google aerial view. You have here a site map. I'm sure you can locate the vehicle on this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I misunderstood your ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, the witness has marked with a dot the place where the vehicle was located at the time it was hit. Witness, as General Praljak says, we can see that there's HVO at the top and ABiH at the bottom. A bullet hits the rear of the vehicle. What enables you to say with a hundred degree certainty that the bullet came from the HVO and not from the ABiH side, given that on looking at this map this could also be a likelihood, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said, I wasn't in the car so I can't categorically say it was from the HVO, but the driver of the car had that firm opinion, and without looking at the report I can't see -- I can't -- I can't link that. I think the -- there's -- there's a good point here, but I can't answer it. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we have the next document, please, IC -- or, rather, before we do that would you place your signature and the date on the map and a number 1 by the point you indicated.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could we have an IC number, please, for the said map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This map will become Exhibit IC 547.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps for the record the first sketch where the witness was asked to supply additional information, that was P 02830. That was the original number, and that was part of a document shown the witness the day before yesterday. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'd like my sketch to be attached to this sketch, too, with an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, we had the sketch, and Mr. Praljak had drawn a circle. Could we have a number for this one too, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the sketch will become Exhibit IC number 548.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I just -- as to that sketch where several joins were made up which about Praljak. I just want to be -- for the record, I want it to be very clear that the witness did not make any drawings on that sketch, and all the drawings on that sketch are Mr. Praljak's drawings and not the witness's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is -- that is correct, Your Honour, but there are comments in the transcript referring to the sketch, so we need a number, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Bench will draw the necessary conclusions thereof. The sketch -- on the sketch on which General Praljak had drawn a circle is sketched number IC 548. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 10000. It's the house. May we go back to that house that you lived in just for a moment. You said yesterday that it was facing west, that the front of the building was facing west, towards the sandbags, and that the sides were towards the north and south. Now, my question is this: From what point in the HVO positions could a bullet arrive to hit the north side of the house? And I think this is a question asked by Judge Antonetti yesterday. So from what side, from what HVO position could a bullet have come hitting the north side of your house and the place that you entered? Let's take a look at the house again. On the left-hand side is the north side. So can you tell the Court to the best of your recollections that in that direction, since the Neretva is down there, there are no HVO positions and that it was all BH army positions over there. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, the shots didn't come from the north. The -- the damage on the north side was from previous conflict or whatever. The shots almost came from a westerly direction and always -- so -- yeah, they always came from a westerly direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, show me on the map the number of bullets that can be seen or just put number 1, 2, 3, 4 how many times was that house hit from a distance at about one an a half metres, sniper shots, sniper bullets?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't low -- I can't recall which of those spots are snipers. I said most that were reported either went through the window shutters or, as I say, landed nearby as either by the vehicle or by the stairwell. And you'd have to refer back to the numerous times that it was targeted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I am bearing all that in mind. I don't think Their Honours are blind. We listened to your testimony yesterday during the examination-in-chief, and you mentioned a whole lot of sniper shooting. So could you then point out -- or, rather when, a bullet hits a facade of this kind it leaves a trace. Would you mark the number of the sniper hits and traces from a distance of 1.500 metres. So take up your pencil and indicate the number of bullet shots, one, two, three, four, however many there are. You are a soldier, sir. You know that you count bullets, you count hits, and they are visible, or traces are visible. So how many can we see on this picture?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, A lot of them went through the windows into the sandbags and into the dirt alongside the steps. Unfortunately, we haven't got a photo of the rails, but maybe they would show more. There is -- I simply can't. I can show you -- I could mark every one of those and say it's -- it's an impact, but there's still many that you can't see in the sandbags or window shutters. Or most of them, as I said, were around the vehicle and on the stairwell. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could you help me out here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see any hit, any impact on the sandbags, and what window was impacted, and can you hit a window from one and a half through metres?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, on the we have before us we see certain traces of impact. As far as the window is concerned, the lower window on the right-hand side, we see the trace of impact. The window above -- below, we see two traces of impact. We do see several traces of impact on the side of this house, on the front side of the house. Can you see them or can't you see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see those impacts but I can't see the sandbags. Also I, need to mention this was taken in June, and at that stage the sniping -- when this photo was taken, which was very early on in my piece as team leader, the sniping at the house itself was at a very low level. At a later date, the observation hole through the -- at the far end was actually changed, and it was moved into the centre hole. So this photo is representative of what the house was like early June. It -- it doesn't reflect what happened for the next eight months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you are saying that this photograph which we have before us is a photograph that was taken in June, and which does not reflect, as far as impacts are concerned, the shots that were fired afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. And I think yesterday that maybe I was asked when that photo was taken, and I think it was June. And as I also said, most of the impacts shown at that time were from previous conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness, who has taken the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one? I took this photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the record I'd just like to note that these three black dots on the window are the points that prevent the blind from coming down. And secondly, we don't know that this was taken in June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the third point, Mr. Finlayson, as a military observer, had a camera, and I think it would be within the -- within your assignment to take photographs in July, August, September, and to attach reports about sniper fire and when your mission was targeted. So I don't want to go back to that now, but may we have the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Just for the record, Your Honour, I object to this comment by Mr. Praljak. That's not a question. It's improper. If counsel did that it would not be allowed. Just Mr. Praljak is asking questions does not give him broader authority to make comments. It's improper. Please instruct Mr. Praljak not to engage in such commentary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the fact that my colleague interrupted at this point, Mr. Praljak mentioned in the sentence that my colleague is objecting to that the points to the bottom of the blinds are the borderline which prevent the blinds from being raised, and I see that the witness gestured and confirmed that. Now, we can't have gestures in the record, but perhaps it would be a good idea to have an oral response, because on the photograph it -- it could be a hit, a point of impact, but on the other hand it could be those points where the blind is prevented from going further up or down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak asked the question that runs as follows: How come that the witness, who in a number of reports has stated that several shots were fired at this building, shots coming from snipers, in those months after the month of June did not take a picture in support of his reports. This is a question that's been put to him. So I'm putting it to you now, Witness. You have drafted a number of reports which we looked at yesterday, and on a daily basis you were explaining that shots were fired at this building. How come that in one of the reports you sent off you did not deem it necessary to take a picture in support of your report and to show to those people who were going to read your reports that this wall where the front part was pitted with bullet holes? As you said, this photograph was taken in June, and the shots were fired after that time. Why did you not deem it necessary to take a picture of this in support of your reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Firstly, Your Honour, the military observers were not given photographic equipment to take photos for their role as military observers. All cameras there were essentially for private use only. There was no means of developing them available to us. I actually take the point that possibly that would have been a good idea in hindsight. However, there are lots of bullet holes you can take pictures of, and I would say now, I guess, if you took a photo of the house it would show a great difference, but as things progressed and it was a normal run of the mill thing occurring. I think an UNMOs report would be substantial enough. They don't report for nothing that a bullet's gone through their accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may -- if I may add a question. Mr. Finlayson, we have earlier had a letter, 3D 00913 of Mr. Lasic as a reaction to your protests. I do not see that in this letter the sniping is actually denied. Now, you have had many conversations. At the end you have even said at one point that it was expressly admitted, and the HVO even took responsibility for sniping. But have -- at other times, have there been protests from your interlocutors with the HVO that there had not been any sniping and that no shots had been fired at that time your house at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, I don't believe that ever occurred, and most -- on most occasions it was -- liability was not necessarily accepted, but it was inferred by the fact that they tended to almost without exception blame uncontrolled sections of -- of the soldiers, HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you say that the HVO took responsibility upon itself. The HVO recognised that there was possible fire, although all this sniper and stories about snipers, well, we'll come back to that, but did the HVO actually say that it took over responsibility in the sense of an order or the intention to shoot at you? That's what I asked you about the guns. Or did it -- was possible that uncontrolled individuals might have shot, as they did from various parts of town individually? When did the HVO take on and recognise its responsibility as being done by the Main Staff, the headquarters of the brigade or whatever else? Will you agree with me that the HVO never recognised that? It recognised its impotence, said that it was not possible for them on a battleground like that in a town like that to control, keep every -- each and every individual under control? Is that the right interpretation of the discussions you had with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interpretation of the discussions we had was the fact they accepted that it was their soldiers and -- and that they would continually say they would issue further orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let's have another document on the ELMO. We'll come back to this event of the 9th of May in due course, which you say was an HVO attack on the BH army in Mostar. Now, take a look at the map on the ELMO now, please. That's the situation prior to the conflict. Can we have a view of the whole map, please. The red is the Republika Srpska army, the green is the ABiH and the blue is the HVO. We have the zone north of Mostar, the zone south of Mostar. You were there. Do you agree that this is what the lines facing the VRS looked like, which were held by the 1st HVO Brigade of north of Mostar, or, rather, the 2nd Brigade north of Mostar, the 3rd Brigade south of Mostar, and the 1st HVO Brigade towards Stolac, and the green parts were held by the BH army, and within Mostar itself there was a separation line which was the Bulevar at Santiceva Street. So, Mr. Military observer of the United Nations, does this map accurately indicate the situation in Mostar prior to the conflict on the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I can't recall the individual brigade numbers. However, the -- prior to the -- May the 9th I would have considered the Muslim -- or ABiH line to be further into the city due to the fact, as was pointed out yesterday, their headquarters was further into town there. So surely that was contained within the area they had control of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, but let me repeat my question. Regardless of the names of the brigades, do you know, you were a military observer, I'm sure you wondered where the lines were facing the Republika Srpska army, does this map reflect the actual situation on the front line facing the army of Republika Srpska, those positions?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could I see the transcript of what he just asked me? I believe those to be, to the best of my knowledge, as the situation was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So we then agree that to the left of Mostar you had the HVO in Bijelo Polje, and to the right of Mostar towards Buna, Blagaj, and so on, was, generally speaking, covered by the HVO. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's generally correct. I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you sign the map, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And could the usher put another document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to object to the witness signing this map. Again, these are all drawings by Mr. Praljak on the map and the witness has been asked on a very general map to confirm that this is the situation, and I can understand that he is hesitant to do so, and I would object for the witness to sign this drawing of this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that these objections to introducing IC material is just a waste of time and they have no sense. You have explained the techniques applied. Let me say again if we are discussing a sketch or any material whatsoever which receives an IC number, which is given an IC number, then it must become part of the exhibit so that in one month, two months, two years, or 20 years' time we can read the records and look at the image or picture, otherwise we won't be able to do that. So that's the only reason, the only point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The map has not been drawn by the witness, admittedly, but on the basis of this map which has been introduced by the Prosecution, the question that is put to him is that whether the front line between the HVO, the ABiH, and the Serbs is the one he has drawn, and the witness has answered by saying, yes, I don't challenge this. I don't challenge the front line. We don't have anything more than that. Whether he signs or not doesn't make any difference whatsoever to what's being discussed here. So, registrar, could we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will become Exhibit IC 549.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- I don't understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- why the witness would have to sign this document. If the witness marks a document or a photograph, then I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said is whether he signs or doesn't, it makes no difference. There is no point on focusing on that. The own reasonable consequence we can draw thereof in the judgement is there is a front line. On the one hand, there are the Serbs; on the other, the HVO and the ABiH. And that's all we can infer thereof. And we can draw the conclusion that the Serbs were close to Mostar. And I can also draw the conclusion that the front line part is occupied by the HVO and then -- the ABiH, and then the HVO. So this map may prove useful from Mr. Praljak's standpoint. I don't know. It's for us to tell him [as interpreted] how useful it is for him. Please proceed, Mr. Praljak. We have five minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know there was something called North Camp near the railway station, North Camp belonging to the former Yugoslav People's Army? And do you know on that on the 9th of May, 1993, in North Camp, there were units of the Croatian Defence Council located there? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I -- I think I recall that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the next document, P 02488, please. P 02488. But may we have an IC number for this map? We don't need a signature. If you want to sign it, you can, but we don't need one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the signature is not essential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't see how we could admit this map. It has not been mentioned. No reference to it has been made at all. You have not asked, and the witness has not confirmed that it shows the North Camp. That question was not put. At least I think the question or to put that we have a link between the map and the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the description of what is shown on the image was given, whether the HVO was in North Camp, and the witness says, "Yes, I think I recall that." So he's confirming the picture. Would Mr. Karnavas like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do believe that Judge Trechsel is correct. Perhaps the gentleman could just look at the picture and see whether he identifies North Camp. Yes or no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to join in Judge Trechsel's objection, and I again state for the record I don't understand some of the reason why these maps are being marked. I understand the President's comments, but it's no different. We don't ask -- when we show witnesses a -- documents, every time we show them a document we don't have them put their name on it. It's an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It has been waived expressly. This time, expressly, it's been said that the witness does not have to sign that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But the point of it is, Your Honour -- I understand that, Judge Trechsel, but the point of it is, is that when we put -- if the Defence wants to draw documents, put numbers on exhibits and use them just like a Prosecution P number, they can show the witness exhibits, but every time we show them a document, we show witnesses tens, 20, 40 documents. We don't have them sign every exhibit that's shown to them. Having them simply put their names on documents on maps is no different, and, frankly, it's -- with all due respect, it's not -- most of this is nothing more than Mr. Praljak trying to shove all these maps in as if they're, you know, as if it's his evidence. He's the one testifying, and it's not proper. And there's no reason to follow this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just very briefly. The gentleman can look at the map that's in front of him. He can then identify exactly where is the North Camp, where he believes it to be, if he can identify it. If he does -- if he does mark it, identify it, then he can initial it because then that is his initial to that mark. Now, if he cannot identify it, the map is still useful because then I suspect that through other witnesses, General Praljak is going to establish where the North Camp is, and then if we have a military observer on the ground who was supposed to know where everything is and can't identify them, then obviously it calls -- it goes into his credibility so that's the usefulness of this so he if he could just identify and mark where exactly is the North Camp, and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the accused General Praljak is showing you a map drafted by him overnight, I assume, because Mr. Praljak has told us that he worked through the night, and he has drawn the location where North Camp is, and he has marked it with 09/05/1993, and HVO. This is the question he has put to you. Is this North Camp? From memory I think you said I think so in the transcript. Let me put the question to you again the map, or the picture as you see it in front of you is this a fair representation of North Camp, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry. Just this whole thing of signatures and not signatures. I'm quite happy to confirm that this is North Camp, but the exact boundaries I can't confirm are exactly as he has drawn there, so hence I wouldn't be comfortable signing it to say that, but I'm quite happy for it to be mentioned in the script that that is North Camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Lines 20 to 25 of page 36, you explain that this must be North Camp, but you cannot ascertain with a degree of certainty that these are the exact boundaries of North Camp. Could we have an IC number, registrar, please, and we have wasted five precious minutes for a subject which was of no particular interest.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this map will become Exhibit IC 550.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's now time to have a break. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Just let me repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it accurate that on the 9th of May, 1993, in the so-called North Camp there was the HVO, regardless of where its precise borders were?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: From memory, that is correct. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must tell you openly what this is about, why am I introducing this. It's about repeating the fact that the HVO were attacking Mostar. I'm telling you so that you can prepare. To the left in Bijelo Polje is an HVO brigade. To the right there's another HVO brigade. There's the HVO in the North Camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: When you were near that tank over there, did you see a general attack on Mostar taking place? Why were those units not involved? What was the point of not getting those units involved? Would not any attack on Mostar would have involved those units from the North Camp from the south, from the east?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is this a question -- is this supposed to be a question to the witness? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And what else but speculation can the answer be, Mr. Praljak? How can the witness know something like that? I think it's not a proper question, I regret, and our President has said we will have a pause, and I think you should respect that. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, all I wanted to tell the witness is that after the break I will be asking him all these questions. We have before us a soldier of 20 years. I will be asking him all these questions. I'm asking him to give it a thought during the break. If I had five hours at my disposal to go through this enormous amount of information provided by this gentleman in his report, well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... we're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. As far as time is concerned, you have another 15 minutes, I believe, Mr. Praljak, and Mr. Kovacic will have 10 minutes. This was schedule. Is that right, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, sir, if you could please answer quickly, given the time limit. From your position from which you viewed the conflict in Mostar, did you see any attack whatsoever from the HVO's North Camp? Did you see the HVO launch any attacks in the direction, for example, of the railway station, or do you simply not remember? Quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't witness any attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any attacks by the HVO to the north of Mostar, the positions held by the 2nd Brigade, any attacks that they may have launched on Mostar? Yes or no, please. From Bijelo Polje, more specifically, any attacks, any movements by units?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were none north of Mostar. There was fighting in Bijelo Polje, but I'm unclear of the lines and which side was instigating it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We're talking about the 9th of May and a little later, but, please. What about the south side, the position of the 2nd Brigade? Did you see any troops, any units, HVO units, moving and attacking Mostar to the south, from the south side?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the south side I didn't have a great view of that, but to my knowledge and from what I did see, I don't believe there was any attack from the south.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. P 02488, please. This is a report of the acting commander of the 2nd Brigade -- the 3rd Brigade of the HVO. The 22nd of May, 1993. Page 1, please. The Judges, I'm sure, will read the entire document, but I'm interested in the last paragraph on this page, the last paragraph on page 1. The number of men of the 3rd Brigade of the HVO with 1.200 soldiers was reduced to 980 men, the reason being units of the 7th, 8th, and 9th Battalions were abandoned by ethnic Muslims. Do you see that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Does this not indicate how many ethnic Muslims there were to begin with in the HVO's 3rd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many ethnic Muslims or Bosniaks were in the 2nd Brigade of the HVO, the one that was stationed in Bijelo Polje? Did you ever come across that piece of information, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question about this: You, as a soldier, would you have attacked Mostar, assuming you had half the 3rd Brigade, who were Muslims, 45 per cent, to be more specific, that's my information, the 2nd Brigade to the north, and you would have remained still in the North Camp. Do you think that would have been a legitimate offensive strategy by the HVO under the circumstances? You as a soldier, would you have done that? Please say, "I don't know," or simply yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object. This is pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I don't think this is a proper question. It's pure speculation, fantasy. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you. I withdraw the question then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could please quickly go through September 1993. The document I need is P 0 -- P 085 [as interpreted]. The date is the 15th of September, 1993. P 05085. Do we have that? Page 3 is the one I'm looking at. It reads: "Jablanica." It says: "10th. The fighting in the battles in the Vrdi area." Have you got that, sir? Page 3 of the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm just looking for reference to Vrdi. What paragraph number?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is page 3 of the Croatian version, and in the English it's page 2. Page 2. It says "Jablanica." It reads: "Tense as reports of fighting ..." Is Vrdi far on the left bank of the Neretva? The hills behind West Mostar. It's the right river bank of the Neretva River, and Jablanica, and I think you took the road across Vrdi to go north occasionally, did you not?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. The next document is P 05234, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask whether we are supposed to have these documents? I haven't found the previous one, and I don't find this one. I don't think they're in your bundle, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is the OTP bundle relating to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We didn't use this exhibit during our direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And you did not submit it, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we -- we didn't -- we didn't submit it to the Court, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I would like to explain this. I noticed when my learned friend, Ms. Nozica, was examining yesterday the OTP this time around did not give you, the Chamber, the same documents that they gave to us, the Defence. To you and to the witness they provided a selection of the documents that were served on the Defence, the selection having been made based on the following criterion: Which documents will be shown to the witness certainly. Therefore, we have twice or three times as many documents as you have. I'm not sure if you can use that as some sort of an explanation or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document P 5234, we have it on the screen, and we'll manage with the screen. Go ahead, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do have to comment. It is known since Monday morning which documents the Prosecution has put at our disposal, and it would have been possible to produce the other documents and let the Judges have them, and I would -- I would appreciate if in the future that were done in this way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we cannot make a final plan for our cross-examination until the witness is finished. We were working on the assumption that you received the same documents from the OTP that we did. It was only yesterday that we discovered this, and even then we weren't sure. I do have a copy of the document, though, and we can have it days played on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there is an assumption being made in your remarks, Judge Trechsel, that we actually know which document they're going to use. We have -- well, we have all these documents, I'm forced to read them, and then, I guess, through their selection process they decide to use. That's their prerogative, but we don't know. And now that we know that you don't have all the documents we'll try to make arrangements, but we're not trying to complicate matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I understand that you do not have a copy of the bundle we have, so you cannot know what is in there. So I withdraw this teaching.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not going to let it go just -- you know, we simply don't accept that every time there's a courtroom -- a problem in the courtroom, it somehow -- it always seems to be the Prosecution's fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nobody's saying it's the Prosecution's fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It sounded like it to me, at least from some counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, it isn't. They gave us more documents than they actually will use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then they have -- there's a selection process during the proofing section. They're entitled to do that. We have more than you have. We don't have the actual list that they present to you. If we have that list, then obviously we know exactly what you have, and then we can decide to provide you with whatever we're going to use from their bundle which they're fault going to use. But nobody is criticising the Prosecution. They're being more than fair to the Defence on this -- on this matter. So I think Mr. Scott should just cool his jets a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, that doesn't help matters when you make those kind of comments, frankly. I appreciate what -- Mr. Karnavas having said that. If I stand corrected on that, I appreciate the comments that apparently they agree we've been -- the Prosecution's been more than fair. But there's a second point, Your Honour, and that is that whatever we do or do not do does not relieve Mr. Praljak from being prepared and providing both the Prosecution and the Chamber with the appropriate documents, and the fact that -- whether or not they're in the Prosecution bundle, it's his responsibility, and -- when he cross-examines the witness to have the documents available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I -- for my part, first I quite agree that no reproach to the Prosecution was anywhere in the air, as far as can see it. But I would suggest that perhaps the OTP serves the Defence with a list of documents, those that they submit to the Judges, and this makes it easier for them then to know what they should add.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We did that, Your Honour. A letter ... Excuse me, Your Honour. I stand corrected on that point. Often we do that. Excuse me. Just so the record's clear. If I'm mistaken, I'm mistaken and I'll admit it in the courtroom. In some cases we do that and I thought we had. I now -- understood that it was not done in this case and I stand corrected indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So once again we have wasted a lot of time on a problem that should be easily solved. On Monday we received from the Prosecution a list of documents in which we do not find Exhibit P 5234. So that when the Defence counsel plan to submit a document not to be found in the list, they know that the Judges do not have that document because it's not mentioned in the list. So as far as possible, the OTP should provide the document. That's all. It's so obvious that it wasn't worth wasting so many precious minutes on this. We don't have the document, but Mr. Praljak is allowed to put his question during his cross-examination. We'll do with what we have. We'll use the e-court system. Mr. Kovacic, you even want to give us a document, or wants to give it to my fellow Judge in case he needs it. Go ahead, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, on page 4 of the Croatian, item (G) -- or, rather, (H), it says: "Assessment of a senior military observer, team leader." Is this you, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says: "The assessment is that behind the apparently unrelated activities in Vrdi, Donja Mahala, and incursions from south Mostar towards Stolac and Capljina, there is a more comprehensive plan at work. If it is confirmed that BH forces are only seven to eight kilometres from Siroki Brijeg, then the outflanking of Vrdi and road access from the north to Mostar may no longer be a speculation." Have you found this, and is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, just one thing. I think this is a very important document. It will be very valuable for the Chamber to be able to go through the document for yourselves. I have these documents prepared for my examination, and I would like the usher's assistance, please, to give the Chamber now those two additional documents, including the one that we are now discussing. The OTP can also have a copy of their own document if this number is missing from their binder. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer my question, please? Is it true what it says here about the BH army activities?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was written at a time when I was just returning to the mission, so the report is not familiar to me, neither is that particular day, so I can't confirm it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will round this subject off, although I could use further documents that were produced after your arrival. I want document IC 00427. That's the document I need right now, and this is the large map that has been used already. Based on your information, sir, can you say whether at the time of your second arrival in late September, 1993, there was a large-scale offensive by the BH army in progress towards Stolac, Hum, and Vrdi. IC 00427.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I recall an offensive against the Hum. I can't recall when that was. And the Vrdi area, certainly there was a mere activity up there, offensive activity, but I could not clarify exact locations of that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There we have the axis of attack on Hum on this map. Can you -- as well as the axes on Vrdi and Planinica, and you mention that in your report. Can you confirm that these axes shown here on this map are accurate? You have the large-scale map right behind you, just in case you want to cross-reference, given the fact that you make reference to Planinica in your report and your team, as well as Vrdi, even Neum, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I cannot -- I cannot confirm the -- the accuracy of that map in the detail it's given. However, as I said before, I was aware that there was offensive at that time toward those point, the Hum anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about towards Vrdi?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vrdi area was very, very difficult to observe, and as I said earlier, I -- there was -- there was activity up there. There was offensives being conducted by the BiH, and that's all I'm prepared to -- to say, because I couldn't accurately portray anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My last question, it seems that I won't be able to go into other documents, unfortunately, already seen by the Court. I need now IC 00042. This is the large map showing the offensive known as Neretva '93. It will turn up as an IC number. My question is: Do you know anything about the offensive conducted by the BH army known as Neretva '93? It started in Konjic and then moved on to Bugojno. There were operations carried out in Uskoplje, and then they advanced further south. Do you, in your capacity as a military observer, know anything about that offensive? If so, please, can you specify what exactly IC 00042, and we have the large-scale map just behind you?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think again just to emphasise that there was activity there and the map you're presenting is showing front lines, which we didn't have access to either by -- due to not being allowed to pass by the HVO or the BiH, so the actual position of front lines, et cetera, was -- the information just simply couldn't be got.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that you weren't familiar with the front lines. Anything is possible, after all. But in your reports there is an enormous amount of this, and then globally speaking as a military observer based on the UNPROFOR information, perhaps, or the reports that you received, did you ever learn about an offensive known as Neretva '93, which started in Bugojno and then they advanced on Uskoplje and Mostar and so on and so forth? Are you familiar with this military blue print for this offensive? I'm not talking about individual sections of the front. And what, if anything, of that plan have you seen as a military observer on the ground?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw -- I do not know of the term Neretva '93. I don't recall it at this time. I do recall the action around Bugojno and Uskoplje, but to be honest, that was at the extremes of my section, and that was actually being monitored very carefully towards the end directly by Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in charge of Rama and Uskoplje, your team, Tomislavgrad, Livno, Uskoplje, Konjic, Jablanica, was your team in charge of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, and -- I'm sorry, it's -- I'm just getting confused, I think, on the locations. I don't think I can answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in charge of Uskoplje and Rama?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that area came under my area of control. Sorry, I -- I just take that back. I -- I'm sorry, I'm struggling on the recollection of the towns and the names of exactly where a couple of these fell, whether they were inside -- they were close to my area of sector, if not monitored by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Unfortunately, on account the time constraints I have no further questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you proceed, I have a question for the witness. I have to put this question to him. Let's go back to the 9th of May, Witness. The 9th of May is an important date, because it's in the indictment. It is said in the indictment that on that day the HVO launch an offensive against the ABiH in Mostar by taking, among other things, the headquarters of the 4th Corps, which was located in the centre of Mostar in West Mostar. You were at the time the UNMO who was present in that area, so I'm talking to the military man in you. Your mission was to provide information to the headquarters in Zagreb as to what was happening on the ground, and I heard in your answers that you were moving about in armoured vehicles in Mostar and outside of Mostar in order to gather information or intelligence, and as you said, this was also based on observations you made from the house where you were located. So when there was a military offensive, and I'm talking to the military here. As you know, things have to be -- have to be prepared. There are plans. You can't I am improvise that altogether, because you need logistics to carry it out. Also, military means have to be put together. Fuel, equipment is needed. So if there is a military offensive, those who are going to launch it will need means. Given your position as an observer, had you noticed that there was going to be an offensive? I compared your diary with your witness statement, the one you gave to the OTP, and I was able to see that you refer to the 6th of May. There is a minor reference to the 8th of May, and apparently on the 9th of may you seem to discover there was an offensive. This was a long question, but I had to preface it with various pieces of information. So given your position as a UN military observer, had you understood that the HVO was about to launch an offensive on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
