utterances.text: Your Honour, firstly I must clarify that on the 9th of May there were no UNMOs in East Mostar or in our house. At the time of the 9th of May, I was an UNMO accompanying General Bo Pellnas. On the 9th of May, our access to Mostar was prohibited by the HVO in the initial stages of the attack. The -- we were able to gain access via a back country road, and that's why I marked on a map, I think on the first day, to the north the position where -- where we observed the 9th of May for. That was not at the time the attack started. Leading up to the 9th of May, I would say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm not interested in the 9th of May. I want to know whether you as an observer, you had information that could lead you to believe that there was going to be an offensive, an attack on the 9th of May, and such information could only have been gathered on the 8th, on the 7th, or in the previous day. You can see that I am putting a different question to you, not about the 9th of May. You expect what you saw on that day. I want to know whether before the 9th of May you had information making it possible for you to believe that there was going to be a large-scale offensive, because if you attack the headquarters of the 4th Corps, and right in the middle of Mostar, this is not a minor operation. I wanted to know from you whether you had information before. Can you answer this?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that stage we -- as we were still conducting the joint commission patrols and -- at that time, so we knew the situation was getting difficult. However, there was no direct knowledge that an attack was going to start that day, or I had no knowledge as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The question also relates to the ABiH, because some say that it was the ABiH that launched the attack, not the HVO. So here again I want to know whether you had information that led you to believe or could have led you to believe that the ABiH prepared an attack on the 9th of May or around that date.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I had that information. However, I comment it would have been suicidal considering the amount of equipment they had at their position, and certainly there was a lot of heavy artillery on the HVO side on the 9th of May which hadn't been there as a matter of course over the preceding weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question, which is only the conclusion of my previous questions. When you discovered on the 9th of May that there was an attack, because -- this is in paragraph 25 of your written statement. You say that you had heard on at that date that the HVO had launched an attack. When you found that out, was that a surprise to you, or did it confirm things? What was your feeling when you heard that there was something happening?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it -- it -- it wasn't expected, but then again, it didn't come as a surprise. I hope that explains. It -- it -- the whole environment was so unpredictable and unstable at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Kovacic -- yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I just may say something before we continue, and this relates to the last question by General Praljak where he asked about these two areas, Rama and Uskoplje being in the area of responsibility of the UNMO, and the witness appeared to be a bit in the dark about these names, and just if I can also say that Rama is the same as Prozor, and Uskoplje is the same as Gornji Vakuf. Would that clarify matters for the witness.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would. Neither of those are in my section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Bos, for that clarification. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm going to take you back to start off with to something General Praljak asked you, and I think that you probably made a slip. And may we have the following document: P 00755 on the screens, please. Anyway, you were shown this document and it was called the "standard operating procedures-UNMO sector BH South." You remember that document, I'm sure. You saw the document, and it will come up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Your Honours, you have the number in our files, and the number is 00755, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you see the document? And I'm going to ask the registrar to put on 818, the last digits, relationship with the local population is the title of that section, and the last digits of the ERN number are 818. And my first question to you, Witness is the following: From the title of the document, it would appear that it was operational procedure precisely for this particular sector in which you spent one year, except for the times that you were in Kiseljak, the three times you were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It was -- yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In fact, I'd just like to draw your attention to point 2 of that operational structure. So may we go back to page 1 of the document, please, Mr. Registrar. And in point 2, it says expressly -- we have page 1 on our screens now so I don't have to read it out for you. You can read it yourself. At the top of the page. Point 2 at the top of the page, please. There, that's right. So point 2, all UNMOs, et cetera, shall familiarise, et cetera. So this is in the imperative mood. It is what the observers are asked to familiarise themselves with; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's as it's written, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So do you stand by the answer you gave, that you've never seen the document?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly stand by I don't recall seeing the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Witness, that you did not in fact follow the instructions and orders given to you by your superiors within your suborganisation or UN sector organisation? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I followed all instructions I had from Zagreb or Kiseljak. All I'm saying is I did not see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday, and from your statement it would emerge that you had a certain amount of preparation first in New Zealand, and then when you game to Zagreb additional training and preparation. So during those preparations, were you given instructions with similar contents, along the lines of what this document sets out in greater detail? And this is dated the 16th of November, 1992. So the document existed when you arrived in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- this UNMO sector BH South document, the standard operating procedures specific to that area, I can't recall ever seeing. The guidance that we got was during our training, I can't recall if we had standing -- I'm -- I'm quite sure on this one. There were standard operating procedures for BH command. But I mean, to be fair, they're probably very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now may we go back to the page with the digits 818, and the top of the page, point 8. Could you read out what it says, "Relationship with the local populace," point 1, "To maintain an image," et cetera. Read it for yourself?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To maintain an image of impartiality, UNMOs should ensure their relationship with local population is one of a professional nature. They should endeavour to ensure that they do not have any close ties with any individuals or organisations."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] Now my question is as follows: Since you say that you don't remember having seen the document either in Zagreb or later on, is this provision something that you learnt through general training and your own understanding of your job, and did you have it as a principle in your conduct and behaviour?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My principle was to maintain impartiality at all times, and I am totally convinced I did that. I, to a degree, encouraged the people with me to communicate with the populace, and that was at a later stage than this, but that was to try and break down the horrific barriers that were being created between UNPROFOR and -- and the populace in some areas. Relationships in -- when you live with people or in a predicament with them develop naturally, but I don't think they ever -- if I ever thought, myself or any of my UNMOs, which I did at times, were become being unprofessional or not -- no longer impartial, I would remove them from the various teams, and that -- that -- that occurred in a number of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Now, Mr. Praljak read out from your diary some excepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we go closed session for a moment, please -- into private session, because I want to refer to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're become in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Today you said, this is for the record, it was on page 6, line 3, that you said two days later a Spanish soldier was killed by the same sniper. You know what I'm referring to, I assume. And my question is this: We have heard here testimony and saw documentary evidence about that unfortunate event when that Spanish soldier was killed. We dealt with that at length, and among other things we learnt that an investigation was conducted into the matter. The UN police took part, among others, and we learnt the investigation was never completed, and we also learnt that it was never established within reason that the HVO -- that the Spanish soldier was killed by the HVO or that the bullet came from HVO positions. So how can you say in this court of law quite resolutely that you know that it was the same sniper who had killed a witness two days ago? Now, it is my assertion or not, so you can agree to that or refute it, that you considered that that was so at the time, but, sir, can you say that with any certainty, or are they simply preliminary conclusions on your part at that time without any further analysis or without any information and proof and evidence in the matter?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly my recollection. Firstly, I think -- I think you can -- you're correct in that I can't categorically say that, and so therefore I change, but the reports and the manner in which they died -- he died indicated from my memory of it, and discussions with the SpanBat at the time was that it indicated that. It was from an elevated position similar to the bank building, but, yes, you're correct. I can't categorically say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Well, thank you for that. Yes, we know that. The substance of the matter was just to see whether you could say with any certainty. Now, for the record, and I have been told that on page 60, line 11 that the following was stated, who had killed a witness two days ago. It was the Spanish officer who was killed. Thank you. And just something else. Not to go back to your diary but, generally speaking, the information you provided through it and, if necessary, we'll refer back to it, but, sir, it was quite clear to you when you came to Mostar in March 1993 that in the bygone period, the period before, while the Yugoslav People's Army and the Army of Republika Srpska or, rather, the Serbs were the active side in the aggression, that they inflicted enormous damage, I think you say "enormous" at one point or words to that effect, enormous damage by a Serb bombing in Mostar, by a Serb shelling in Mostar. Do we agree on that point?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that is the situation that you encountered when you arrived. That's how things were; right?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now something else that emerges from the material, without entering into detail, although we can do so if need be. Is it true and correct as you say that the Serbs from time to time shelled Mostar during the time that you were there, which means during 1993 mostly?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early stages they used to shell up by the dam, and every so often we tended to get the very occasional impacts from the Serbs. I think from memory from -- my teams did report the odd -- a couple of days where there were more than five or maybe 10. I can't recall the exact number, but very -- and relative during my period, relative to all the other incoming and outgoing artillery, et cetera, rounds, it was a minute level, absolutely minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Defence is addressing an important issue for the Judges. You have just said that as far as you know the Serbs shelled Mostar on several occasions. What I'd like to know is this: As far as you know, did the Serbs also have snipers? Did these snipers shoot at Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I didn't hear any -- have any reports of snipers from Serbs except for I just say guardedly that possibly in the very first month I was there, there might have been some unconfirmed reports of sniping by the Serb, but that was when the armija and the HVO were together. But for the bulk of the time, certainly May, June, right through to the time I left the mission, I can't recall any -- any reports of Serb sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And just one more question in this connection. Based on your knowledge of the -- of where all three parties in the conflict were deployed in the area around Mostar and in Herzegovina, I assume you would agree that Mostar, throughout 1993, remained within the range of the JNA artillery or, rather, Serb artillery, because the positions and the Serb lines did not change. Just a short answer, please. Did they remain there or not, and remain within range or not?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want to go on to a different area, but unfortunately I've taken up too much time already, although I do think it would be interesting if we were to show the witness his readiness, et cetera, but -- well, maybe just one more question. I've been just prompted by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In view of the indictment and the allegations in the indictment, it is clear, Witness, from what you've said so far, but I'm responsible for the transcript, let me ask you, were you personally ever wounded in that entire period in Bosnia-Herzegovina, actually, in Sector South? Were you injured or wounded? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You obviously weren't killed either because you're here with us. What about any of your colleagues, colleagues from your mission? I think there were about 25 of you there. You were there for a year. What about your colleagues, were they wounded or injured or anything?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my time in BH South I had no injuries, but I'm sure looking at the photographs it was more good luck at times than management. There were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of course, luck, this -- something emotional, mental. The fact is, though, you were not wounded, and as far as I can tell it you're quite alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the sake of an explanation, in paragraph 115 of the indictment, the -- the witness was cited as a victim, whereas he was clearly not wounded. I do have to point this out, although that should be sufficiently clear based on all the documents and the testimony so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So far you've had four hours and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, sir, there's one thing that I would like you to answer. This question was asked by my learned friend Mr. Kovacic about your wounding. You said you weren't wounded yourself, but he asked you about your colleagues, too, whether any of them were in Sector South during their time there. We received no answer to that, so could you please tell us, sir.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no military observers wounded. However, there were a significant number of Spanish soldiers injured or killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had agreed with my client that he would use up the last five minutes of our cross-examination for his questions. He, however, has now asked me to start, and I respect his desire, so if the Chamber could please allow him the first five minutes now. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to Your Honours. Cross-examination by the Accused Petkovic:

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to the witness. My name is Milivoj Petkovic. I conferred with my counsel about my need to ask certain questions that follow from Mr. Praljak's questions about September 1993. I would like to ask the witness this: Sir, is it true what you said in your statement that on the 21st of September you arrived in Medjugorje, and you were a senior military observer ever since? From Kiseljak, I mean.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a period of hand-over, but essentially that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that there is always some sort of a hand-over. Let me ask you about that. You arrived on the 21st. I do assume that you first read the reports by your colleague in relation to the previous day. Would not be something that anyone would expect you to do in a situation like that?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I can't remember if I read the report or was given a full brief, but certainly I would have been made aware of that, that -- the occasions on the day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Among other things, you received all the documents; right?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would have been available to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. General Praljak asked you about the 29th [as interpreted]. The document is P 05234. It says: "Assessment by the senior military observer." And your answer was simply that you weren't there. Was that your answer, that on the 29th you weren't there? That was your answer, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it the 29th? I don't think so, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The 29th, yes, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, there must be some mix-up, because the document that Mr. Praljak has quoted, P 05234, is dated 20 September. Mr. Prlic -- THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] The 20th of September. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: September 20th. When it is said in Croatian it means 29th. So September 20th. General Petkovic spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is obviously an error in the transcript. Instead of the 29th it should be the 20th of 9th month, the 20th of September, 1993. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, your colleague who handed over his position to you the next day I'll read to you what General Praljak has already read to you. He concluded in relation to you that day that the assessment was that there were apparently unrelated activities in Vrdi, Donja Mahala, and problems in south Mostar towards Stolac and Capljina. There was a master plan behind these seemingly separate activities. It is confirmed that BH forces are only 7 to 8 kilometres from Siroki Brijeg, then the outflanking of Vrdi and road access from the north to Mostar may no longer be a speculation. Is this an accurate reading of what your colleague wrote down?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me now move on to a different document, dated the 21st, another conclusion by a military observer. I'm not sure if that was you or your colleague. The document number is P 05263. That is page 8 in the Croatian, and I'm not sure about the English. This is under H. Just below that it reads "Sarajevo." That's just for ease of reference. I can perhaps read what your colleague or you wrote on the 21st in your assessment and your conclusion. "Yesterday's offensive of the BH army does not appear to have resulted in the taking of much territory. It did, however, cause tensions to rise among the HVO forces, and it did succeed in exerting pressure on military elements. The assessment is that yesterday in the Vrdi area, the BH army forces did not advance to the south to the extent that was reported, and it appears that in Mostar they are not in control of Donja Mahala. This uncertain situation, it appears, will go on for several days." So this is the conclusion made by military observer in relation to the 21st. In your conclusion, do you speak about the BH army offensive, or are you trying to assess its results, whether it was a successful one or not?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I -- I don't believe I particularly wrote this one, but that's an assessment of the results at the end of the day I would have read it as.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I did say that. Maybe it was you. Maybe it was one of your colleagues. As a soldier, I value this assessment much more than the first five points. It's a strategic assessment. You agree, don't you?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, one thing I don't know is about P 025285. If so, I'll just skip it. If not, I would like to move on to another conclusion made by a military observer in order to prove that military observers make strategic conclusion, assessments as to what exactly was going on as part of that operation. I'm not sure if that document has been submitted already or perhaps we should place it on the ELMO. Sorry? P 05285. I'm willing to drop the document if the Chamber has no copies. So this is P 05285. I'm not sure. Because of this confusion I do not wish to cause any problems. I do, however, believe it to be an exceptionally important document. It's a document produced by the military observers, of all people. Can we have P 05285.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document has not been prepared for your benefit. We didn't believe that we would be using it. I do have an English copy, and if that could please be put on the ELMO. If I could have the usher's assistance. If he could give us a hand with that. Here is the entire document, but the reference will be just to the final point of the document, which is the assessment itself. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Item (C), "Meetings." That is the portion of the document that I'm interested in. It's page 2 on my copy, and I'm not sure about the English. The next page, please, (C). Under (C). Witness, could we please look at (C). It says: "Meetings: MX6," which is your team, "met with LO," liaison officer. "Team informed BiH forces attacked Rastani, Donja Mahala, and several other places in town across the confrontation line and also trying to take Planinica." We asked you a while ago about Planinica, didn't we. "Confirmed BiH forces took Rastani yesterday." And this isn't substantial about you meeting in Capljina with the Capljina Brigade. And now on to item (H), "Assessment." You say: "The reported BH attacks at Planinica, Donja Mahala, Rastani and other areas indicate a gradual offensive to occupy some of the vantage mills and strategic positions around Mostar. The HVO would not surrender these areas and heavy fighting is expected in the next few days. "BH intentions around Vrdi are not fully understood ..." This is obviously your own conclusion, because on that day you were supposed to be taken over. Is this an accurate conclusion made by the military observers at the end of that particular day?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's an accurate conclusion. However, I must confirm you're in error in assuming that it was me that wrote that report. If you look at the start of the report, the SMO at that stage is still Lieutenant Colonel Espensen. I don't doubt anything that is said there. It's --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. But it was produced at or -- at around the time of the hand-over; right? So you were both familiar with that; right? All the better, I say?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Witness, these are your documents and --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we could just ask the witness to once again repeat the answer since the answer was not recorded. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said the report was accurate; right?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I showed you three of your reports in which you indicate that there is a BH army offensive afoot north of Vrdi, Planinica, Mostar town, and to the south Donja Mahala. You know all of these locations, don't you?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm struggling with Planinica, but I think I mentioned earlier that I was familiar with an armija offensive to the north and the south, so -- which confers with this, but I couldn't rather the details and I still can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. But you don't know, do you, that this was part of Neretva '93, part of that military OP operation? You don't know that, do you? It doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that name being used, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please, Witness, in order to confirm the veracity of your allegations, I will now show you a BH army document. This is an order to carry out an attack. The number is 3D 00736. For the benefit of the Chamber, this number as well as other documents have been used during earlier cross-examinations. 3D 00736. Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An explanation for the Chamber since I see they're trying to find the document in our own set. These are General Praljak's documents. I'm not sure whether they were prepared for this witness or not. So could we please start looking at that binder. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] My apologies, and I wish to thank my counsel for assisting me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have before you an order written by the -- a commander in the Mostar area. He happens to be the commander of operations group Centar, which you refer to as being part of the rally, say, that the 1st Brigade came Centar. That's what you wrote in one of your reports. This order was approved by Mr. Pasalic, because it stemmed from one of his own orders, which is under 3D 00740. That's for the benefit of the Chamber. Can we please go to item it 2 of this order. Sir, item 2 reads: "The task of operations group Centar is to launch an attack on the downtown area and to take over the following axes." The first being quoted is the electric power plant of Mostar, Rastani village, Orlac. The next one is Semovac Podhum, first elementary school. The third one is the Hum facility, H-u-m facility. The fourth axis is Donja Mahala-Stotina-Rodos. Can you look down, six or seven lines down, where it says, "Readiness for the attack by 2400 hours on the 19th of September, 1993." As a soldier, when this term is used readiness by this or that hour, what exactly does that mean? Does that not mean that an operation might start at any time after that time? Would that be a correct assessment?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I would read it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Item 4. Item 4 was always a decision, according to the rules of the previous army. So this -- this commander decides to carry out a vigorous attack by grouping his main forces along the following axis: The Hum facility, Podhum, the Mostar water plant, Rodos, and Rastani and Orlac. Those are the main forces and the auxiliary forces along the following axis: Santiceva Street and retirement home. B and R, I'm not sure what that means. Bulevar Naranavero Lucijer [phoen]. That's an abbreviation. The high school building, you were looking at that today, and the health centre it. "The objective being to cross the enemy forces along the axes of attack by our forces, inflicting losses in terms of manpower, equipment, and materiel, while at the same time creating conditions for final launching of operations to liberate the town." Have you been following the interpretation, sir? Is my reading accurate?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: There is no need for me to go into all the other orders. Praljak is helping me, and he's suggesting to have a look at artillery, which is item 8. "Artillery support for this attack will be secured by the battalion firing group along the axes of attack of the battalion," which means that each battalion has a battalion firing group, and a -- the mixed artillery decision of the 41st Brigade artillery battalion will be providing fire support, according to a plan drawn up by the commander of the operations group Centar. So, when you link the next document up with your own report and with the orders produced by the BH army, will provide us with a comprehensive context. Are you familiar with this? Do you know that this is what things looked like at the time? Or is this the very first you hear of it, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the -- the attacks on -- on some -- some of these places, but off the top of my head the dates are unsure, but they certainly appear to match up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You see the commander of operations group Centar wrote this down in the log, Mr. Sejtanic. The document is 3D 00736. 3D 00736. We won't be going through the whole log, just certainly elements. The page is 3D 22-0387.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: 0687, correction. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: For ease of command over units of the 4th Corps, the following units were set up: Operations group south, operations group south 2, Mostar Centar, operations group north, and so on and so forth. The one that we've heard mentioned here so far is operations group Centar. I'll read on. "Defence lines were established against the Serb forces but were not active in terms of combat. However, the smuggling was rife along those lines, smuggling including all kinds of items, especially food items, that were missing." And then the next page: "Based on information provided by soldiers indicating that Sefer Halilovic was in Jablanica with forces from Bosnia, one started singing the following song," and I won't be reading the song. I'll move on to the item that reads as follows: "As part of the preparations for the upcoming combat activities, there was open discussion of the possibility that the Serb side would help us in terms of direct artillery support and in terms it of supplying necessary equipment and items, particularly a large number of -- of artillery missiles of different calibres." And it goes on to say: "I attended a meeting along the confrontation line with the Serb forces in the village of Busak

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: defined the conditions under which the Serb side would be assisting us in combat activity." And then I'm moving on to the next page: "As for our cooperation so far, Safet Orucevic spoke to the commander of the Nevesinje Brigade, Novica Gusic, and gave him a present of a nearly new Golf car, JX." Now I'd like to come to the following passage where it says: "In the period from the 10th to the 18th of September, intensive reconnaissance work was carried out of the objects of attack, and then towards the end it goes on to say: "During the 19th of September we once again analysed the information obtained and looked to see how preparations were conducted and became informed of the combat operations that were launched by the BH army units along the axis of Dreznica, Vrdi, and Goranci." And then it goes on to say: "During the night, without any problems, units were brought in to the town of Mostar from whence in the early morning hours they were supposed to move towards the objects of attack. The unit which attacked at Hum hill was led by my deputy Tahir Brajic [phoen]." And then it goes on to say: "The combat activities started in the early morning hours of the 20th of September, and they followed planned dynamics, especially along the flanks where we expected to be successful and which we would use to prolong the operations on the town itself. The combat operations were particularly successful at Visnjica, Hum, Rastani, Jedrinje and features around Vrba [phoen]." And now to the next section. It says: "The units in the town nucleus scored initial success along the axis towards the Barinovac [phoen] settlement," which is below you. No it isn't. Ah, it's opposite. Right. Now, listen to this, please: "And faced with strong artillery Serb support, there was success in sight." And let me repeat this, because you said that on that day there was a lot of bombing of Mostar, and with a large-scale or strong Serb artillery support we had every chance of success. On the basis of following conversations over the radio link, HVO and HV [as interpreted], and they were amazed, additionally, with the knowledge that the Serb side was directly assisting us in the operations." Now I'd like to skip over a section there because he says that they received an order to cease hostilities, and then he says at the end: "We strongly attacked Commander Pasalic for stopping the fighting, and we accused and blamed him that he was in cohorts with the official policy in Sarajevo an and was digging a grave for Herzegovina and that trust in him as a commander --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This has been going on for a long -- quite some long time, and if it's all going to mean, did I read the document correctly, did I read it correctly it's not going --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to note that they do not have the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to put right an error in the transcript. On page 75, line 9, it wasn't the HV, the Croatian army, but the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] And just one more sentence and I'll complete that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: "The consequences of the combat operations, the units of the 4th Corps, were terrible. During the withdrawal to the initial positions, we had more than 30 dead. About 100 were wounded, whether seriously or less seriously," et cetera. Now, Witness, in your reports for this period in Mostar you wrote about the fighting and about HVO shelling, said that the HVO was shelling. Now, from the documents, did you see that the BH army had agreed to provide strong support to the Serbs or with the Serbs? Did you -- were you able to see that there was this strong support?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that document, as you read it out because I haven't seen it, yes, I can see that that's certainly indicative -- indicated within that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, anywhere in your document did you make mention -- or in your documents, did you ever mention that you had any knowledge about the contacts between the Serb and Muslim sides up at the front line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this question must be split up. He has not yet said that he had such knowledge. So first, did he have the knowledge? Second, did he report about it, please. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just for the record, the question that was ultimately put confirmed my concern, cause at the end of the day, the only question that was -- essentially was, did I read that correctly? And the witness said that appears to be what the document said. So there was in fact no question, no real question to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. Petkovic raised the -- put the question. So put the question again, Mr. Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, on the basis of your own documents and combat documents of the BH army that we have seen and also the books issued by the commander, can we conclude that in September the BH army launched an attack on a broader area of Mostar, and around Mostar, including the town of Mostar against HVO units?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports produced by BH South UNMO didn't indicate any Serb support. That report is compiled through the reports of the observers who would have been in Mostar at that time. Whether that is an error or not I can't comment on, and unfortunately our reports were reliant on our people reporting what they saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me repeat my question between. From all this, is it evident that in September, starting with the 20th of September, the BH army launched an operation against Mostar and the area around Mostar, including Vrnik [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My objection is the same as before, Your Honour. This is nothing but a long speech, reading by Mr. Petkovic. There's no basis for this witness to answer the question. It's not even a proper question. I mean, there have been some limits, Your Honour, and today it appears there are no rules, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question was not properly put, but the meaning of it is very clear. And I'm going to ask this question of you, Witness. General Petkovic read out a document that said the ABiH launched an attack with the support of Serb artillery. This is the case put by Mr. Petkovic. As far as you are concerned, you and the other members of the UNMO team, to your knowledge did you know of the attack launched by the ABiH, attack that would have been supported by Serb artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to go off the reports that came from my sector, Your Honour, and they didn't indicate that we were aware of it. I seem to recall that the report from the UNMOs reported the offensive in the north, but indicated that the offensive in Mostar was in retaliation. Did I got -- I haven't got those in front of me at the moment, but the document that Mr. Petkovic has just produced would tend to indicate that possibly their -- their observations were incorrect, and that can't be discounted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 20 to 1.00. We're going to break for 20 minutes. We shall resume at 1.00 for another 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to continue. Please proceed, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to thank you for giving my client five minutes for the cross-examination and for allowing him to extend that five minute time limit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, to start off with, I'd like to clarify some details linked to your meetings with General Petkovic and when you contacted General Petkovic with respect to the attacks on vehicles and facilities of your own institution. Let me remind you, and please correct me if I'm wrong, so far you've told us the following: That the complaints about the attacks on the vehicles and facilities of your institution, you relayed to General Petkovic and asked to give concrete examples. You mentioned the incident at Siroki Brijeg when one of your vehicles was stopped and searched, but you couldn't remember when that actually happened. Now, my questions will exclude the 18th of April, 1993, when there's no doubt that you saw my client arrive at the meeting that was held then. Now, my summary of your testimony about General Petkovic, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meetings at Citluk, I believe, I attended at least one, but from memory the majority of the discussion was from my Ghanaian deputy who also wrote that letter to him as a follow-up. But I think I indicated earlier that I recalled having meetings with General Petkovic but couldn't, in fact, remember when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, you couldn't remember a single specific event apart from the incident at Siroki Brijeg, which I mentioned, and what you said was recorded on pages 90 to 91 of the transcript of the day before yesterday. But let's take first things first. You mention a document which refers to the incident at Siroki Brijeg. It is a document that we've already seen in this courtroom. You can take a look in my set of documents. The number is P 05990, and it is a complaint dated the 21st of October, 1993, which was sent to the head of the Main Staff of the HVO in Citluk. Tell me, please, Mr. Finlayson, was that the document that you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one I was referring to, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Fine. With you now take a look at another document that I have selected at random for you to be able to see who was the chief of the Main Staff at that time, the chief of the HVO Main Staff. So take a look at document P 06091. It is a document which the Chief of the Main Staff issued on the 25th of October. That is to say four days later, four days after the document we talked about a moment ago, and tell me, please, Witness, who is the signatory as chief of the Main Staff at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigadier Tole, and he is who I actually recognise as being the Chief of Staff. It jogged my memory there but I ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Witness, did you otherwise have any dealings with Mr. Zarko Tole? I don't know how to decline his surname, but anyway, did you hear of him before? Did you have contacts with him?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I -- in fact, I only say that because I've read my diaries through, and I mention it in one case where I was trying to gain access to the southern part of the sector. To be perfectly honest, I cannot recall Mr. Tole. I didn't meet with him often enough to be able to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now if I might refresh your memory, I'd like to refer to the diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So may we go into private session for that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, since the meeting with General Tole -- with Brigadier Tole was a few days after the written complaint with regard to the attack on the UN vehicle, I'd like to ask you whether it is possible that you might have discussed the incident with General Tole, which was the subject of the written complaint.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I believe, as I said before, the discussion -- this particular issue was taken up with Mr. Petkovic by my deputy SMO at the time. It may have come up in conversation, but the primary reason for that visit to Brigadier Tole was to gain access.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us, Witness, how come you would send a written complaint to Brigadier Tole and after that your deputy with General Petkovic discussed the issue.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been priorities at the time, and I think at that time the priority or that I was being requested to get sorted out was the -- whether or not there was HV in the -- in the area. The -- the issue of continual attacks on -- on UNMOs was very important, but it wasn't, I guess, of strategic importance as far as UN strategy at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you then explain how these questions of strategic importance would have been discussed with Brigadier Tole, whereas matters of marginal importance you would discuss with General Petkovic? Was that the usual way you would communicate or they would communicate with the UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, we -- I can't answer that accurately, but brigadier -- we often got referred to local areas regarding getting into for operations in a particular area. We found to -- typically we would -- an operational issue we would concentrate on the local -- the local parties. We found that more effective, in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in view of what you've just said, where is the place and role of General Petkovic in all this? What was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Petkovic at that time, I understand, was the commander of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This notion of HVO commander doesn't mean anything to us unless you specify, because Brigadier Tole, too, was also a commander. So could you specify? Was he a commander for a local area or a broader area or you just can't remember what post General Petkovic held at that time, which is also quite understandable?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly my notes had that Brigadier Tole was in fact the Chief of Staff. The -- all my references, I think, to General Petkovic was that he was commander, HVO, and I didn't elaborate on that, and I can't recall. Certainly my understanding through all the meetings that we had had with General Pellnas, he -- the understanding was he was responsible for the majority of Bosnia, but that's probably a bit late in the piece for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to remind you, if possible, that in April 1993, when the meeting was held, the meeting where you discussed this and when agreements on a cease-fire were signed, that on behalf of the Croatian side, or, more exactly, the HVO, those documents were signed by Mr. Petkovic, who at the time was the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO. Therefore, what you wrote during part of your term of office is one thing, and it's another what happened after that. So do you know up until what time General Petkovic was the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall -- recall that at all, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. What I'm actually interested in is this: I'd like you to be specific and precise. If you claim that your deputy contacted General Petkovic, linked to the complaints about the attack on your observers, can you tell us when and where your deputy met with General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding -- my recollection is he met in Citluk and -- but the dates I would not be able to recall without reference to the official reports from UNMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, according to your knowledge were there any written traces of those meetings, the meetings between your deputy and General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as memos or a minute goes, I don't believe so. However, it would have -- that would have obviously been reported in the daily military observer reports, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, if in those daily reports we do not find a piece of information about your deputy's meeting with General Petkovic, would we then be able to conclude that the meeting never took place?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Although we can now definitely confirm -- well, you say that you personally never had a meeting with General Petkovic; is that right? Did I understand you to say that?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I had one in Citluk with General Petkovic and, however, I can't recall what the topic was. I just recall having a meeting there with General Petkovic, and I think Colonel Lasic might have been there, but at what time in my deployment I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Witness, General Petkovic at that time was the deputy HVO commander. In your diary would you have recorded a meeting with the person who was a deputy or the number two man in the army -- of the army?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The diary, unfortunately, that you've got, it's a personal diary, and I have found that it is -- I have found it frustrating that I didn't put details in on certain days, and I can only -- well, I know that on certain days there are other things going on and I had little time to jot something down, so not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then let's move on. Witness, you mentioned an incident to us with Arif Pasalic on the 8th of May, 1993, and you said that he, if I'm going to reproduce this correctly, was on his way back from Jablanica towards Mostar, and he was stopped at a check-point on the north side of Mostar, and after that he was able to continue along his way. That's what you said. And he might have got out of the vehicle outside Mostar. But in brief, he was not allowed to stay in Mostar. Did I interpret the incident correctly, or do you wish to correct me in any part of the statement I've just made?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my -- my recollection of it was he was prevented from returning to Mostar that evening from a joint commission meeting either in -- in the Konjic-Jablanica area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Another time he was on his way back down the Jablanica-Mostar road and on to Capljina. Is that the road he took on his way to Mostar, or was it a different road that he took at the time? Did he take that road that you called the Sarajevo-Split road or the Jablanica-Capljina road?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- that's my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir, is that the road you mentioned as passing near that house that you rented in June where you set up an office? Is that the road?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, let's assume this situation: A vehicle with Arif Pasalic is stopped at a northern check-point held by the HVO. The vehicle then continues down the same road through East Mostar. A six-kilometre stretch of that road is -- is under the control of the BH army. Why did Arif Pasalic never leave the vehicle while in East Mostar given these facts?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- that -- that road between Mostar and Jablanica, from memory, the front line at that time intersected it probably about four times where it changed from armija to HVO hands. I seem to remember we used to probably go through four different check-points at various times. My understanding is that he was prevented at an HVO check-point on the way down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, are you trying to say that he was not stopped at a northern check-point to the north of Mostar but, rather, as he was on his way out of East Mostar and on to south Mostar?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I can't comment on that. My understanding, or my recollection of the reports relating to that was that he was stopped north of East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we then conclude, regardless of the fact whether he was stopped north or south, that in both cases Arif Pasalic would have been free to stay in East Mostar, had he chosen to do that?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he was stopped north of East Mostar, he wouldn't have been able to stay in Mostar. He wouldn't have got there. If he was stopped south, he would have already passed through. So obviously he would have been free to stay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir, Witness, he certainly passed the northerly check-point, because he was eventually driven to the south of the Mostar area. That is a fact. It's indisputable. He was not returned from the northerly check-point and told to go back to Jablanica. He passed on his way through Mostar and all the way to the south of the Mostar area, but can you please first comment on this?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You obviously have more information than I have in my recollection, so I -- I would not want to comment any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Let us move on and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Ms. Alaburic, but you're moving on to another topic. It's important to me to raise the following follow-up question with the witness. We see that on the 8th of May, General Pasalic, who was the commander of the 4th Corps, that is the highest authority of ABiH in Mostar, as he was crossing check-points, be it in the north or in the south, it doesn't really matter to me right now, he was controlled by the HVO. Whilst listening to you, I asked myself whether if there is -- if there was a large-scale HVO operation on the 9th of May, how come they did not think of arresting their opponents on that day? For instance, for catching -- to catch General Pasalic as he was crossing a check-point. And if so, if there was indeed a large-scale operation to be conducted by a classic army, in theory, General Pasalic, since he was crossing a check-point, the HVO authority should have been informed of it and they could easily have arrested him. And they had done so, that would have been sort of preventing by beheading the opponent. You were a senior officer. How can you explain that General Pasalic was allowed to go through on the 8th of May whilst a few hours later, and we've seen evidence to the effect, at 3.00 in the morning there was an action that was carried out. How can you account for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to be careful that I don't speculate here, but my -- my understanding is that he was in a joint commission patrol at the time, in which case he would have been inside a Spanish APC. I think I'm getting in a dangerous area here where my recollection may -- may differ to -- to the facts, so we may not be wise to continue too much. But that was my understanding, but I would honestly have to read the -- read the reports to try and get the recollection. Remember, at this stage, I -- there wasn't a team in East Mostar. However, I was aware of this unfolding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You aren't therefore in a position to answer this in military terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have to ask you another question about this same matter. We have just referred to SpaBat. We saw the documents. We know that General Pasalic was taken to this place called Dracevac. That is south of Mostar in the general direction of Capljina. What I want to know is if he was on his way from Jablanica, could he have reached Dracevac by taking that very road through East Mostar that was under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us move on to the 9th of May. I'll try to be relatively brief, because you have already confirmed for General Praljak that you were familiar with the fact that the confrontation line between the BH army and the HVO in Mostar ran along the following line: Bulevar-Spanish Square-Santiceva Street. This is page three from today's transcript. Is my interpretation of your words correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think my -- my comment was generally -- I think I actually mention that the precise position of the front line. At -- at what point on the 9th of May are we talking about? I think I also mentioned that the BiH line possibly should have been further into the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can jog your memory. The question was this, and I'll read it in English: [In English] "Do you agree that the separation line, correct me if I'm wrong, the Bulevar up to Spanski Square, and then Santic Street is the area marked and was that, to your knowledge, indeed the separation line? "No -- sorry, yes. I do agree that was the separation line as I knew it." [Interpretation] Could we now try to define this. When was that confrontation line established separating the BiH and the BH army? Could you also please have a look at a document in my binder; this is 4D 557. This is a report by Arif Pasalic, dated the 20th of April, 1993, being sent to the President of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, and the staff of the BH army. At item 1 -- I'll just refer to this portion that is about the confrontation line. The line is defined as follows: Semovac, the Bulevar, and Mose Pijade Street. People from Mostar know that the Mose Pijade Street was later renamed Kolodvorska street. Are you familiar with that street, Kolodvorska street?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd certainly need a map. I can't recall the names of the streets now without a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I do have a map ready to use, but Kolodvorska street is not particularly prominent in this map so maybe we'll use it later. But there is something I really want to know right now. Let us try to ascertain this. Did you have any information to suggest that as early as the 20th of April, 1993, there were decisions and reports about the fact that there was a confrontation line running through Mostar town itself? Were you aware of this confrontation line as early as April 1993, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 20th of April I was a mere driver and I didn't know about the confrontation line at that point or I can't recall it. I do recall at that time that the teams were dividing or separating and developing zones, but a clear definition of those I would -- I didn't have a knowledge of, and I don't know if it was known by anyone in the UN at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the interpretation of my question where the term being used is "confrontation line," which perhaps is, is not the best interpretation possible. It may not be possible to find a better term right now. My learned friend is suggesting the term "division line." So I suggest we leave it to our interpreters to judge what's best. Item 2 of Arif Pasalic's report suggests the following, and you were asked questions at great length by my learned friend Ms. Nozica about this, the fact that all the units belonging to both armies will be in their own facilities without assuming any combat positions, with the facilities being guarded, guards standing outside. Is this portion of the report consistent with the negotiations that we discussed about withdrawing units to their respective barracks and the withdrawal of the BH army to Konak and to the area known as the South Camp?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is along those lines, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on your memory, sir, the meeting was chaired by General Pellnas. We see that in item 4. Or do you perhaps not remember who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do remember who was in charge, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything at all about the fact that on the 10th of May, 1993, Presidents Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic agreed a cease-fire, and each of them issued a statement. The documents are for you to consult in my binder, and the numbers are as follows: 4D 00456, and 4D 00457. What about Mr. Pellnas and -- and the other officers among the UN military observers? Do they have any knowledge of those statements issued by the two leaders?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that if they were issued they would have known about them. There were numerous cease-fire and numerous agreements, but to -- if this is a legitimate document, I would -- and there was still some -- the 10th of May, I'm not too sure whether we could still get into Mostar, but I'm sure communications at the higher level would have ensured that they had these. But that's speculation. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. This agreement between the army leaders General Halilovic and General Petkovic, dated the 12th of May, this is something you're testimony with. You report this in your diary, something to that effect. You remember the agreement, don't you?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's in my diary --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we please try to verbalise your smile. That's right. Thank you. So that's right. That would be the answer. When you think back to what was going on in May after the 12th and 13th, could we conclude that the rest of May was relatively peaceful, that there were incidents of sporadic exchanges of fire by both sides and some later incidents, but said on the whole relatively peaceful. As a UN military observer, would you assume that to be a correct assessment of the situation?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout this war the term "relatively" is -- is quite misleading. Relative peaceful compared to the heavily -- sorry, heavy attacks in the preceding days. Essentially it did quieten down, but I think for a full appreciation of what action was still -- still occurring you need to refer to some of the UNMO reports at that time, which would be -- which would clarify the impacts or the activities itself. But essentially the main activity was in those few days, and I don't believe it increased too much until, I think, June there was another bit of a stouce.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm trying to use the observations and the wording from your report. For example, the reports from September 1993, those reports state a full-scale war has broken out. Your colleagues from UNPROFOR in their reports emphasise that the events in your area were in some way related so that the events in Konjic and Jablanica affected what weapon in Mostar and around Mostar. Do you share those observations, or do you believe that these are two totally separate areas that did not mutually affect one another?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- they were always obviously related. I guess the -- the problem is finding out what -- what occurred first, what came first.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: A while ago you mentioned that after a relatively peaceful continuation in the month of May, 1993, the situation degenerated in June of the same year. Therefore, can we please look together at P 02750. It's an OTP document. It's an UNPROFOR report dated the 14th of June, 1993. We can have a look together and see what exactly happened around Mostar that might have had a bearing on what then occurred within Mostar itself. Can we start with the addendum to this memo, which is page 12 in the B/C/S and page 10 in the English.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have a look at that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If the usher could please assist us with this. Are we all right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you cannot continue because it's time to stop, and there's a hearing in this courtroom this afternoon. You will have to resume tomorrow, and you can address this question tomorrow again. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could just trouble the Trial Chamber. I would like to very briefly raise one issue while the witness is present. It relates to the confidentiality of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we should go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 10th day of May, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
